questions.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data in the table?

options.A: The share of workers in industry rises steadily as GNI per capita rises.
options.B: Industry employs the largest share of workers in the country with the highest GNI per capita.
options.C: Each country with a higher GNI per capita has a smaller share of its workers in agriculture.
options.D: Germany's high GNI per capita comes mainly from its large share of workers in industry.
options.E: Ethiopia and India have similar GNI per capita because their service sectors are the same size.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Industry's share does not rise steadily: Vietnam (33.5 percent) has a larger industrial share than Mexico (25.0 percent) or Germany (26.4 percent), which have higher GNI per capita.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Germany has the highest GNI per capita, but services, not industry, employ the largest share of its workers (72.4 percent).
rationales.C: Correct. Among the five countries shown, higher GNI per capita goes with a smaller share of employment in agriculture. Ordered by GNI per capita (Ethiopia, India, Vietnam, Mexico, Germany), the agricultural shares are 62.2, 43.5, 27.0, 12.0, and 1.2 percent. This describes a relationship in the table; it does not by itself establish a cause.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The table gives employment shares, not each sector's contribution to national income. Most German workers (72.4 percent) are in services, and Vietnam has a larger industrial share (33.5 percent) with a much lower GNI per capita, so the table cannot support this claim.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Their service shares are nearly equal (31.5 percent), but their GNI per capita is not similar: India's (9,710 dollars) is more than three times Ethiopia's (3,060 dollars).

questions.explanation: Line the countries up from lowest income to highest: Ethiopia, India, Vietnam, Mexico, Germany. The percentage of workers in farming drops every step: 62.2, 43.5, 27.0, 12.0, 1.2. These are shares of all workers, not the number of farm workers.

questions.stem: A student uses the table to conclude that almost every person in Germany has a higher income than almost every person in Mexico. Which of the following is a limitation of the data that makes this conclusion unsupported?

options.A: GNI per capita measures government income, so it leaves out what households earn.
options.B: GNI per capita leaves out income from farming, so it understates income in Ethiopia and India.
options.C: GNI per capita divides national income by the number of workers, not by each country's total population.
options.D: GNI per capita measures output inside a country's borders, so it leaves out income that residents earn abroad.
options.E: GNI per capita is an average, so it does not show how income is distributed among people in each country.

rationales.A: Incorrect. GNI counts the income of the whole economy, including households and businesses, not just the government.
rationales.B: Incorrect. GNI includes income from all sectors: agriculture, industry, and services.
rationales.C: Incorrect. GNI per capita divides national income by total population, not by the number of workers.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Measuring output inside a country's borders describes GDP. GNI equals GDP plus income residents receive from abroad minus income paid to nonresidents.
rationales.E: Correct. GNI per capita divides total national income by total population. The AP course framework lists income distribution as a separate measure of development because an average can hide large gaps between rich and poor within a country.

questions.explanation: GNI per capita divides a country's income by its population. It is an average, not the amount each person receives. Two countries with very different averages can still overlap: some people in the lower-average country can earn more than many people in the higher-average one.

questions.stem: Vietnam has a larger share of its workers in industry than any other country in the table. Which of the following most likely contributed to this?

options.A: Foreign firms have built factories in Vietnam's industrial and export-processing zones to use lower-cost labor.
options.B: Vietnam's industry consists mainly of quaternary research jobs that pay higher wages than Germany's.
options.C: Germany's factories use more workers per factory than Vietnam's, which keeps Germany's share small.
options.D: Vietnam adopted import substitution, closing its economy to foreign trade and foreign-owned firms.
options.E: Germany's workers have moved into agriculture in large numbers, which has lowered the share of German jobs in industry.

rationales.A: Correct. The AP course framework notes that outsourcing has increased jobs in newly industrialized countries and that new manufacturing zones, including export-processing zones, have created an international division of labor. Since the late 1980s, foreign investment in export factories, such as electronics and clothing plants drawn by Vietnam's lower labor costs, has created many industrial jobs. This is a likely contributor; the table itself combines manufacturing with other industry and does not isolate the effect of foreign investment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Quaternary research jobs are services, not industry, and wages in Vietnam are much lower than in Germany.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Employment per factory does not by itself set industry's share of all jobs. That share also depends on the number of factories and on employment in other industries and sectors.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Vietnam moved away from a closed, state-run economy beginning in 1986 and has welcomed foreign trade and investment.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Only 1.2 percent of German workers are in agriculture, so workers have not shifted into farming.

questions.explanation: Foreign companies have built factories in Vietnam to make goods for export, partly because wages are lower than in places like Germany. Vietnam also set up special zones to welcome them. Those jobs help explain why a big share of Vietnam's workers are in industry. The table alone cannot show how much of that share comes from foreign-owned factories.

questions.stem: A lending group offers small loans without collateral to women in rural villages, who use the money to start businesses such as tailoring shops and food stalls. Which of the following best explains how programs like this can improve standards of living?

options.A: The new businesses mainly sell their goods overseas, which brings foreign money into the villages.
options.B: The loans come from the International Monetary Fund, which also requires new schools and clinics.
options.C: The new businesses draw large foreign-owned factories, which often hire village workers at high wages.
options.D: Women earn income that they control, which is often spent on food, health care, and schooling.
options.E: The loans require borrowers to move to cities, where they can find factory jobs that pay higher wages.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Tailoring shops and food stalls funded by microloans mostly sell to local customers, not overseas buyers.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Microloans come from local lending groups and banks. The International Monetary Fund lends to national governments.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Small local businesses rarely draw large foreign factories, which follow large, concentrated investment that is often planned or encouraged by governments.
rationales.D: Correct. The AP course framework notes that microloans have given women opportunities to create small local businesses, which have improved standards of living. Income that women control is often spent on food, health, and children's schooling.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Microloans help people start businesses where they already live; they do not require moving to cities.

questions.explanation: A small loan helps a woman start a business in her village. If it does well, she earns money that she controls. Women often spend that money on food, medicine, and school for their children, so the whole family's life gets better.

questions.setLabel: Questions 13–14 refer to the table below.

stimulus.title: WOMEN'S HEALTH, EMPOWERMENT, AND WORK IN FIVE COUNTRIES (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
columns: Women's share of seats in the national legislature (%)
stimulus.description: Table of five countries. Country J: 410 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, 95 births per 1,000 women ages 15 to 19, women hold 12 percent of legislative seats, labor force participation 38 percent for women and 79 percent for men. Country K: 140; 52; 22 percent; 45 and 77 percent. Country L: 9; 8; 41 percent; 61 and 68 percent. Country M: 25; 18; 28 percent; 52 and 70 percent. Country N: 60; 30; 33 percent; 30 and 72 percent.
stimulus.note: Labor force participation is the percentage of women or men ages 15 and older who are working or are looking for and available for work. The GII also uses women's and men's secondary education levels, which are not shown here.

questions.stem: Based only on the indicators shown, which country's data are most consistent with a low Gender Inequality Index (GII) value, meaning less gender inequality?

options.A: Country J
options.B: Country K
options.C: Country L
options.D: Country M
options.E: Country N

rationales.A: Incorrect. Country J has less favorable reproductive-health and legislative-representation indicators than Country L, along with a much larger gap in labor force participation (41 percentage points).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Country K does better than Country J, but its maternal mortality, adolescent births, and gap in labor force participation are all worse than Country L's.
rationales.C: Correct. The GII combines reproductive health (maternal mortality and adolescent birth rates), empowerment (women's share of legislative seats and secondary education), and labor-market participation of women compared with men. Country L has the lowest maternal mortality and adolescent birth rates, the highest share of women in the legislature, and the smallest gap between women's and men's labor force participation rates (7 percentage points). Education data would also be needed to calculate actual GII values.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Country M has less favorable reproductive-health and legislative-representation indicators than Country L, and its labor force participation gap is larger: 18 percentage points rather than 7.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Country N has a fairly high share of women in the legislature, but it has the lowest women's labor force participation (30 percent) and the largest gap with men (42 points).

questions.explanation: A LOW GII means women and men are closer to equal. Country L has the fewest maternal deaths and teen births, the most women in the legislature, and the smallest gap between women's and men's work rates. Those are signs of lower gender inequality in the measures shown. The table does not include every measure used in the GII.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of using the table's labor force participation data to compare women's economic roles in the five countries?

options.A: The data are percentages, so countries with larger populations appear to have more working women.
options.B: The data leave out unpaid work in the home, such as caregiving and housework, much of which women do.
options.C: The data measure women's seats in the legislature rather than the number of women who work.
options.D: The data include men's rates, which are not needed to compare women's roles in the five countries.
options.E: Labor force participation is part of the HDI, so it should not also be used to describe gender gaps.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Percentages adjust for population size, so a larger population does not by itself raise a country's participation rate.
rationales.B: Correct. Labor force participation counts people who are employed (including self-employed people and people helping in a family business) and people who are looking for and available for work. Unpaid caregiving and housework for one's own household are not counted, even though women do most of this work worldwide, so the data do not measure all of women's economic contributions.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Legislative seats are a separate column. The labor force participation columns describe work.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Men's rates are needed: comparing women's and men's rates is what shows the gender gap in labor-market participation.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Labor force participation is not one of the HDI's measures, which cover health, education, and income. It is part of the Gender Inequality Index, which is built to describe gender gaps.

questions.explanation: The labor force includes people with jobs or their own businesses and people looking for work. It leaves out unpaid cooking, cleaning, and caring for children and older relatives at home. That is real work, and women do most of it, so these rates do not show all the work women do.

questions.stem: In Country B, more women have finished secondary school and taken paid jobs outside the home over the past thirty years. Which of the following changes would most likely occur in Country B during the same period?

options.A: The share of workers employed in agriculture would increase.
options.B: Women would earn more than men in most jobs.
options.C: The infant mortality rate would rise.
options.D: Average family size would grow as household incomes rise.
options.E: The total fertility rate would decline.

rationales.A: Incorrect. More women finishing school and taking paid jobs is not linked to a rise in farm employment; the clearest expected change is a decline in fertility.
rationales.B: Incorrect. More women finishing school and entering paid work does not mean women earn more than men; gender pay gaps usually persist.
rationales.C: Incorrect. More education for women is associated with lower, not higher, infant mortality.
rationales.D: Incorrect. As women's education and paid work increase, families usually have fewer children, not more.
rationales.E: Correct. When women stay in school longer and work for pay, they tend to marry and have children later and have fewer children overall. This is one way changing roles for women are connected to economic development.

questions.explanation: Women who stay in school longer and have jobs usually start families later and have fewer children. So the fertility rate goes down.

questions.stem: Country T is building its first modern roads and ports, banks are beginning to lend money for new businesses, and a class of entrepreneurs is emerging, but most people still farm. In Rostow's model, Country T is most likely in which stage?

options.A: Traditional society
options.B: Preconditions for take-off
options.C: Take-off
options.D: Drive to maturity
options.E: Age of high mass consumption

rationales.A: Incorrect. A traditional society is mainly subsistence farming with little investment in infrastructure or new businesses.
rationales.B: Correct. In Rostow's preconditions stage, a country builds transportation and other infrastructure, develops banking and investment, and gains an entrepreneurial class, while most of the economy is still agricultural.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Take-off begins when a few manufacturing industries grow rapidly. Country T is still building the foundations for that growth.
rationales.D: Incorrect. In the drive to maturity, industry spreads across many sectors and the economy is no longer mostly agricultural.
rationales.E: Incorrect. High mass consumption is the final stage, with widespread consumer goods and a large service sector.

questions.explanation: Country T is getting ready: roads, ports, banks, and business people. But most people still farm, so the fast factory growth of take-off has not started yet. That is the preconditions stage.

questions.stem: According to Wallerstein's world-system theory, which of the following best describes the semi-periphery?

options.A: A stage that countries pass through on their way to the age of high mass consumption
options.B: Countries whose economies depend mostly on exporting one or two raw materials or cash crops to the core
options.C: Countries with both core and periphery processes, exploited by the core but exploiting the periphery
options.D: The countries where most of the world's largest corporations have their headquarters
options.E: Countries that remain outside the world economy and trade very little with other countries

rationales.A: Incorrect. Stages that lead to high mass consumption are part of Rostow's model, not world-system theory.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Heavy reliance on exporting a few raw materials is typical of the periphery.
rationales.C: Correct. In Wallerstein's world-system theory, the semi-periphery mixes core and periphery economic processes. It is exploited by the core but in turn exploits the periphery, and it can act as a buffer between the two.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Headquarters of the largest corporations are concentrated in the core.
rationales.E: Incorrect. World-system theory treats all countries as part of one interconnected capitalist world economy.

questions.explanation: In world-system theory, the semi-periphery is in the middle. These countries mix core and periphery activities: they may make some higher-value goods while also supplying lower-wage labor for companies based in the core. Their position is between the core and the periphery in global trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common criticism of dependency theory?

options.A: It ignores the role that colonialism played in shaping the economies of former colonies in Africa and Asia.
options.B: It assumes that countries pass through the same five stages of growth that Britain followed.
options.C: It explains where factories locate mainly by comparing the costs of moving raw materials and products.
options.D: It struggles to explain how some former colonies, such as South Korea, grew into high-income economies.
options.E: It argues that more free trade with core countries is the fastest way for poor countries to develop.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Dependency theory places colonialism and its legacy at the center of its explanation of underdevelopment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A single sequence of stages is Rostow's model, and this is a common criticism of Rostow, not of dependency theory.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Comparing transport costs of raw materials and products describes Weber's least cost theory.
rationales.D: Correct. Dependency theory holds that unequal ties with wealthy countries keep former colonies poor. Critics argue that strong versions of the theory have trouble explaining former colonies such as South Korea (a Japanese colony until 1945) that became high-income economies. South Korea's experience suggests that government policy, education, investment, and access to export markets can help a country change its position.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Dependency theory warns that trade with the core can keep poor countries dependent; support for freer trade is associated with neoliberal policies.

questions.explanation: Dependency theory says unequal relationships with rich countries hold former colonies back. But South Korea was once a colony and is now a high-income country, helped by education, investment, and selling goods abroad. Critics say the theory has trouble explaining success stories like that.

questions.stem: With the same amount of labor, Country A can produce four times as many laptops as Country B but only twice as much coffee. Assume these ratios stay the same and shipping costs are small. Based on comparative advantage, which outcome is most likely?

options.A: Country A produces both goods, because it is more efficient at making each of them.
options.B: Country A specializes in laptops and Country B in coffee, so both can gain from trade.
options.C: Country A specializes in coffee, because its advantage over Country B is smaller there.
options.D: Country B specializes in laptops so that it can catch up to Country A's technology.
options.E: The two countries do not trade, since Country A is better at producing both goods.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Country A has an absolute advantage in both goods, but comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, so Country A gains more by focusing on laptops.
rationales.B: Correct. The AP course framework identifies comparative advantage as a basis for trade. Country A's productivity advantage is greater in laptops (4 to 1) than in coffee (2 to 1), so its opportunity cost of making laptops is lower. Country B has the lower opportunity cost for coffee. If each specializes and they trade at prices both find worthwhile, both can gain.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Country A's productivity advantage is greater in laptops, which gives it the comparative advantage in laptops, not coffee.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Country B's comparative advantage lies in coffee, where it is least behind Country A.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Different opportunity costs create chances for trade that benefits both countries, even when one country has an absolute advantage in both goods.

questions.explanation: Country A's advantage is 4 to 1 in laptops but only 2 to 1 in coffee. So Country A gives up the least by making laptops, and Country B gives up the least by making coffee. If they trade at a price both think is fair, both can end up better off.

questions.stem: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay founded Mercosur in 1991 to reduce tariffs and other barriers to trade among themselves. Mercosur is best described as

options.A: a cartel that limits production to control the world price of a commodity
options.B: an international lender that sets conditions on loans to indebted countries
options.C: a global organization that settles trade disputes among most of the world's countries
options.D: a union whose member states share a single currency and a central bank
options.E: a regional trade bloc that promotes freer trade among neighboring states

rationales.A: Incorrect. A group of producers that coordinates output to influence prices describes OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lending to indebted governments with policy conditions describes the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Settling trade disputes among most of the world's countries describes the World Trade Organization (WTO).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Mercosur members keep their own currencies. A shared currency and central bank describes the euro area of the European Union.
rationales.E: Correct. Mercosur is a regional trade bloc in South America formed to reduce trade barriers among its members. Its members keep their own currencies, so it is not a monetary union. The AP course framework lists Mercosur among the organizations that foster greater globalization.

questions.explanation: Mercosur is a group of neighboring South American countries that made trade among themselves easier by cutting tariffs. That makes it a regional trade bloc.

questions.stem: Country X places a 25 percent tariff on imported steel. Which of the following best describes the most likely effects on steel-producing towns in Country X (local scale), on factories in Country X that use steel (national scale), and on foreign steelmakers (global scale)?

options.A: Steel towns gain jobs; steel-using factories pay less for steel; foreign steelmakers sell more in Country X.
options.B: Steel towns gain jobs; steel-using factories pay more for steel; foreign steelmakers sell less in Country X.
options.C: Steel towns lose jobs; steel-using factories pay more for steel; foreign steelmakers sell more in Country X.
options.D: Steel towns lose jobs; steel-using factories pay less for steel; foreign steelmakers sell less in Country X.
options.E: Steel towns lose jobs; steel-using factories pay more for steel; foreign steelmakers sell less in Country X.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The tariff raises the price of imported steel, so steel-using factories pay more, not less, and foreign steelmakers sell less, not more.
rationales.B: Correct. At the local scale, steel-producing towns may gain jobs because domestic steel faces less competition. At the national scale, factories that use steel, such as automakers, pay higher prices. At the global scale, foreign producers sell less steel in Country X. The AP course framework notes that government initiatives such as tariffs affect economic development at all scales.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Protection from imports tends to help domestic steel towns, not cost them jobs, and higher prices for imported steel mean foreign steelmakers sell less.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Domestic steel towns are protected from cheaper imports, so they are more likely to gain jobs, and steel-using factories pay more for steel, not less.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Steel-using factories do pay more and foreign steelmakers do sell less, but the tariff shields domestic steel towns from import competition, so they are more likely to gain jobs than lose them.

questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax on imports. Foreign steel gets more expensive, so people buy less of it. Steel towns at home may gain jobs. But factories that use steel, like car makers, now pay more for it.

questions.setLabel: Questions 22–23 refer to the graph below.

stimulus.title: MANUFACTURING AND SERVICE JOBS IN METRO AREA R, A CITY IN A CORE COUNTRY, 1970–2020 (HYPOTHETICAL DATA)
stimulus.description: Line graph from 1970 to 2020 for Metro Area R, a city in a core country. Manufacturing jobs fall from 480 thousand to 430, 350, 270, 220, and 200 thousand. Service jobs rise from 620 thousand to 760, 900, 1,080, 1,250, and 1,390 thousand.

questions.stem: The trends shown in the graph best illustrate which of the following?

options.A: Deindustrialization
options.B: Agglomeration
options.C: Import substitution
options.D: Rostow's take-off stage
options.E: Commodity dependence

rationales.A: Correct. Deindustrialization is a decline in manufacturing's role in an economy, often measured by its share of jobs. In Metro Area R, manufacturing jobs fell from 480 thousand to 200 thousand while service jobs rose, so manufacturing's share of the jobs shown fell from about 44 percent to about 13 percent.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Agglomeration is the clustering of firms to share labor, suppliers, and infrastructure. The graph shows a shift between sectors, not clustering.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The graph shows no import barriers or policies to replace imports with local production, so it does not show import substitution.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Take-off is a period of rapid growth in a few manufacturing industries. Here manufacturing is shrinking.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Commodity dependence is reliance on exporting a few raw materials, which the graph does not show.

questions.explanation: Factory jobs in Metro R fell from 480 thousand to 200 thousand, so manufacturing became a much smaller part of the city's jobs. That is deindustrialization. Service jobs grew during the same years.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most important limitation of the graph for judging how these changes affected the standard of living of workers in Metro Area R?

options.A: It does not show whether service jobs are in the central city or in the suburbs.
options.B: It does not separate manufacturing jobs by the types of products made.
options.C: It does not identify which service firms are locally owned or foreign owned.
options.D: It does not show pay, benefits, or whether laid-off workers found new jobs.
options.E: It does not compare these employment trends with those of other metropolitan areas.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Where jobs are located can affect access to work, but it does not show how workers' pay or benefits changed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Product categories do not show the earnings and benefits that go with the jobs.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Ownership alone does not show workers' pay or whether laid-off workers found comparable jobs.
rationales.D: Correct. Standard of living depends heavily on income. Job counts do not show job quality or what happened to the workers who lost manufacturing jobs. Many new service jobs pay less than factory jobs did, while some, such as finance or technology jobs, pay more.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Comparing with other metropolitan areas would not supply the missing information about these workers' pay.

questions.explanation: The graph counts jobs, but it does not tell you how much those jobs pay or what happened to the people who lost factory jobs. A worker who loses a good-paying factory job and takes a low-paying service job is worse off, even though the total number of jobs went up.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) operate across geographic scales?

options.A: The UN enforces the goals by fining national governments that miss their targets for each goal.
options.B: The goals apply to periphery countries, while core countries are exempt from meeting them.
options.C: The goals measure economic growth, so environmental and social targets are left to each city.
options.D: The goals replaced national governments as the planners of local transit and finance projects.
options.E: The goals are global, but progress depends on national and local efforts like transit and small loans.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The SDGs are voluntary commitments. The UN tracks and reports progress but does not fine countries.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The SDGs, adopted in 2015, apply to all UN member states, including core countries.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The SDGs include environmental and social goals, such as clean water, gender equality, and climate action, not just economic growth.
rationales.D: Incorrect. National and local governments still plan and carry out projects; the goals guide and measure progress.
rationales.E: Correct. The SDGs set shared global targets, but progress happens and is measured within countries and communities. The AP course framework gives small-scale finance and public transportation projects as examples of the kinds of development the goals help measure.

questions.explanation: The SDGs are one set of goals for the whole world. But the actual work, like building a bus line or giving small loans, happens in countries, cities, and villages. Global goals, local action.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the degree to which ecotourism supports sustainable development in a threatened rainforest region?

options.A: It protects the forest mainly by replacing local workers with tour staff brought in from abroad.
options.B: It speeds up deforestation, because tour companies clear the forest to plant export crops.
options.C: It can protect forests and create local jobs, but crowds and foreign-owned lodges can limit gains.
options.D: It helps forests mainly where governments keep local people out of protected areas, so it creates few local jobs.
options.E: It shifts the region's economy toward manufacturing, which adds jobs but also adds industrial pollution.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Ecotourism's benefit depends on employing local people, which gives them a stake in protecting the environment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Ecotourism depends on keeping natural environments intact; clearing forest would destroy the attraction.
rationales.C: Correct. The AP course framework notes that ecotourism frequently helps protect threatened environments while providing jobs for local people. Its benefits can be limited, however, if too many visitors damage the environment or if much of the income goes to companies based outside the region.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Ecotourism usually depends on local people working as guides, cooks, and lodge staff. Keeping residents out would cut their jobs and participation, so it is not a reliable way to meet ecotourism's social and economic goals.
rationales.E: Incorrect. Ecotourism is a tertiary (service) activity. It shifts work toward services, not manufacturing.

questions.explanation: Ecotourism can be a win-win: the forest is protected and local people get jobs. But it only works so far. Too many visitors can harm the forest, and if outside companies own the lodges, much of the money leaves the area.
